documentation.summary: Blind testing methodologies — IV&V, mutation testing, property-based testing, and fuzz testing — share one principle: the verifier must not be biased by knowing how the implementation was built. IV&V enforces organizational independence (separate personnel, budgets, reporting chains). Mutation testing provides mechanical blindness by silently changing code and checking whether tests detect the change. Property-based testing generates inputs the developer never specified, finding 50x more mutations per test than handwritten unit tests per OOPSLA 2025. Coverage-guided fuzzing generates inputs guided purely by unexplored code paths, not developer intent.

examples.title: mutmut: Run mutation testing on a Python module
examples.description: Runs all mutations against the test suite and reports survivors (tests that failed to catch code changes). Scores above 80% indicate strong fault-detection.
examples.code:
pip install mutmut
mutmut run
mutmut results
# Shows only surviving mutants (tests that didn't catch changes)
# Example output:
# SURVIVED: src/parser.py:42: x > 0 => x >= 0

examples.title: cosmic-ray: Python mutation testing with kill matrix
examples.description: Cosmic Ray generates mutants using 9 operator types and provides a kill matrix showing which tests kill which mutants. Useful for identifying redundant tests and coverage gaps.
examples.code:
pip install cosmic-ray
cosmic-ray init config.toml mymodule tests/
cosmic-ray exec config.toml
cosmic-ray dump config.toml | python -m cosmic_ray.reporting.full_text
# Operators: AOR (arithmetic), LOR (logical), ROR (relational),
# LCR (logical connector), constant replacement, unary insertion

examples.title: Hypothesis: Property-based test with pytest
examples.description: Hypothesis integrates natively with pytest via @given. Generates inputs automatically and shrinks failures to the minimal reproducible case. Saves failing examples to a local database so bugs do not hide behind randomness in CI.
examples.output: When a property fails, Hypothesis shrinks to the minimal failing example and saves it to .hypothesis/examples/ for deterministic replay.

examples.title: Atheris: Coverage-guided fuzzing for Python
examples.description: Atheris wraps libFuzzer to provide coverage-guided fuzzing for Python. It instruments Python bytecode for coverage tracking and generates inputs guided by unexplored code edges.
examples.code:
pip install atheris

import atheris
import sys

def TestOneInput(data):
    fdp = atheris.FuzzedDataProvider(data)
    value = fdp.ConsumeString(10)
    try:
        my_parser(value)
    except ValueError:
        pass  # Expected
    except Exception as e:
        raise  # Unexpected exception = potential bug

atheris.Setup(sys.argv, TestOneInput)
atheris.Fuzz()

# Run: python my_fuzz_target.py -max_total_time=60
examples.output: Crashes, unexpected exceptions, and sanitizer violations are reported with the exact input bytes that triggered them.

examples.title: DO-178C: Independence verification by DAL level
examples.description: DO-178C requires that the person verifying software artifacts is NOT the person who authored them. Verification must be requirements-based (derived from specs, not from reading code).
examples.code:
# Independence requirements by Design Assurance Level:
# Level A (Catastrophic): 16/31 review objectives require independence
# Level B (Hazardous):     7/31 review objectives require independence
# Level C (Major):         0/31 independence required
# Level D (Minor):         0/31 independence required
#
# Key rule: Tests derived from HIGH-LEVEL REQUIREMENTS, not source code.
# Verifier reads: requirements docs, architecture, design docs, source code.
# Verifier does NOT start from: developer's mental model, implementation intent,
# or the developer's own test cases.
examples.output: Documented in the Software Verification Plan. Applies to requirements review, design review, code review, and test case review.

common_patterns.when_to_use: When verifying safety-critical or mission-critical software where implementation bias could mask failures. Mandatory at DO-178C Level A/B.
common_patterns.example: Derive test cases from requirements documents only. Do not read the implementation before writing tests. Write expected behavior based on the specification, then run against the implementation.

common_patterns.pattern: Mutation Score as Test Quality Gate
common_patterns.when_to_use: After any test suite is written — especially AI-generated tests. Use mutation score to prove tests actually detect behavioral changes, not just execute code.
common_patterns.example: Target mutation score >= 80%. A score of 4% with 100% line coverage means tests are structurally executed but behaviorally blind. Run mutmut or cosmic-ray before accepting any test suite.

common_patterns.when_to_use: For any function where you can state a general truth about behavior across all valid inputs: roundtrips, commutativity, idempotency, size preservation, consistency with reference implementation.
For any code that processes external input (parsers, deserializers, API input validation, file format readers). Finds crashes and unexpected exceptions on inputs nobody thought to write tests for.
common_patterns.example: Use Atheris + FuzzedDataProvider to generate semi-structured inputs. Run for 60-300 seconds. Even a short fuzz run covers millions of input variations.

common_patterns.when_to_use: When formal certification or high-stakes verification is required. Requires separate personnel, separate management chain, separate budget.
common_patterns.example: IV&V team derives expected behavior from requirements docs. Reports findings directly to project management — not through the development team lead. At NASA: reports to the Chief Software Management Authority.

common_patterns.when_to_use: When debugging property-based test failures. Hypothesis automatically shrinks complex failures to minimal reproducible cases.
common_patterns.example: If a 1000-element list triggers a bug, Hypothesis shrinks to the smallest list that reproduces the same failure. Saved to .hypothesis/examples/ so the minimal case replays deterministically in CI.

gotchas.issue: 100% code coverage does NOT mean tests verify behavior
gotchas.solution: Always run mutation testing alongside coverage. A test suite with 100% line coverage and 4% mutation score executes every line but catches almost no bugs. Coverage measures execution; mutation score measures correctness verification.
gotchas.example: HumanEval-Java study: LLM-generated tests achieved 100% line/branch coverage but only 4% mutation score — missing corner cases like leap year date handling.

gotchas.issue: Tests with no assertions survive all mutations (mutation score 0%)
gotchas.solution: Mutation testing immediately exposes this: if every mutation survives for a test, that test has no behavioral assertions. Fix by adding explicit assert statements that check return values, state changes, or side effects.

gotchas.issue: Mutation testing is slow on large codebases
gotchas.solution: Use incremental mutation analysis (PIT supports this). Run mutation testing only on changed files in CI. mutmut is fastest at 1,200 mutants/min; cosmic-ray supports distributed execution for large repos.
gotchas.example: mutmut run --paths-to-mutate src/core.py  # Only mutate specific file

gotchas.issue: Hypothesis health checks fail on slow strategies
gotchas.solution: Use @settings(suppress_health_check=[HealthCheck.too_slow]) or increase max_examples cautiously. For complex data structures, use st.builds() with targeted strategies rather than generating all fields randomly.

gotchas.issue: Atheris requires Linux or macOS (no Windows support)
gotchas.solution: Run fuzzing in CI on Linux containers. Use OSS-Fuzz integration for continuous 24/7 fuzzing. For Windows development, use a Docker container for fuzz runs.
gotchas.example: Supported: Python 3.11-3.13 on Linux (32/64-bit) and macOS. Not supported: Windows.

gotchas.issue: IV&V verifier bias from reading implementation before writing tests
gotchas.solution: Write test cases from requirements documents BEFORE reading the implementation code. The verifier reads the spec and states expected behavior independently. Only then compare against actual implementation output.
gotchas.example: DO-178C mandates this: tests must be requirements-based, not source-code-based. The verifier should be able to write tests with only the specification in hand.

research_notes.confidence_reason: High: NASA official docs and DO-178C references are authoritative. OOPSLA 2025 is peer-reviewed. Trail of Bits and Meta Engineering are expert practitioners. Mutation tool speed metrics from 2025 benchmarks (medium confidence — vendor-reported). Atheris AI-code specific 2025 data limited (tool fundamentals well-covered, AI-specific applications extrapolated).
gaps: DO-178C full standard text not directly accessible — referenced via Vector and AdaCore whitepapers
Specific NASA IV&V report exclusion lists not publicly documented — inferred from independence principles and SWE-141
Atheris-specific 2025 benchmarks on AI-generated code not found — general fuzzing effectiveness used

key_findings.property_based_testing_effectiveness: Each property-based test finds ~50x as many mutations as the average unit test (OOPSLA 2025 empirical study)
key_findings.llm_test_quality_gap: LLM-generated tests can achieve 100% line/branch coverage at only 4% mutation score — mutation testing is essential for AI-generated test validation
key_findings.do_178c_independence_threshold: 16/31 verification objectives require independence at Level A (catastrophic); 7/31 at Level B (hazardous)
key_findings.mutation_score_target: Scores above 80% indicate strong fault-detection capability in Python codebases
key_findings.mutmut_speed: mutmut: 1,200 mutants/min, 88.5% detection rate — fastest Python mutation tool
key_findings.meta_llm_deployment: Meta ACH tool (LLM + mutation): 73% engineer acceptance of generated tests across 4 major platforms in late 2024
